classification.difficultyReason: Checks supplied values by substitution, including negative numbers, fractions and decimals.

questions.mappingNote: All parts directly assess verification by substitution: a checks addition; b negative substitution; c brackets; d a fractional value; e both sides; f a negative value on both sides; g fractional expressions on both sides; h a sum of fractions; i decimal expressions on both sides.
questions.methodNote: Page 1, Example 1 checks a proposed solution by substituting into LHS and RHS and comparing their values. Page 2 provides supporting equation context; cross multiplication on page 5 is not needed for these checks.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Checks supplied values by substitution, including negative numbers, fractions and decimals.

classification.difficultyReason: Straightforward inverse operations, including negative coefficients and negative solutions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d use addition or subtraction; e–h use multiplication or division; j divides by a negative coefficient. Parts i, k and l follow the page-2 method for a negatively signed unknown. The negative-coefficient skill is the most advanced directly assessed skill in this shared task.
questions.methodNote: Perform the same addition, subtraction, multiplication or division on both sides. Page 2 demonstrates explicit inverse operations and moving a negatively signed unknown to the other side before solving.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Straightforward inverse operations, including negative coefficients and negative solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Applies two or more inverse operations to equations containing fractions, negative coefficients, grouping and decimals.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c and e–f use successive inverse operations; d and i–l use the positive-coefficient rearrangement shown in Example 3(d); g–h add denominator removal and coefficient division; m–p remove the denominator before isolating x; q and s use the same operations with exact decimals; r and t divide by the outer decimal factor before undoing the inner operations. The most advanced assessed items require three inverse operations, so solve-linear-3-step is the closest primary catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Perform equivalent operations on both sides. Example 3 teaches successive inverse operations, multiplication to remove a denominator, and moving a negative unknown term to the other side to retain a positive coefficient. Example 5 supports dividing by an outer factor before expanding when convenient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies two or more inverse operations to equations containing fractions, negative coefficients, grouping and decimals.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand brackets, collect like terms and solve, including negative coefficients and fractional answers.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 directly assesses bracket expansion and multistep linear solving. Negative multipliers in b, d, f and h require correct sign handling; c, d, g and h require collecting terms after expansion.
questions.methodNote: Perform equivalent operations on both sides. Page 4, Example 5, teaches expansion followed by collecting terms, and permits dividing by the bracket multiplier first when appropriate. Parts e and f use that division-first method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand brackets, collect like terms and solve, including negative coefficients and fractional answers.

classification.difficultyReason: Gather pronumerals from both sides, including negative and decimal coefficients and bracketed expressions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–l directly practise Example 4's method with integer, negative and decimal coefficients. Parts m–p additionally require Example 5's bracket expansion. The primary skill is solving equations with the pronumeral on both sides; bracketed parts also assess three-step linear equations.
questions.methodNote: Perform equivalent operations on both sides. Example 4 gathers the unknown on one side and omits routine intermediate operations where clear. Example 5 expands brackets and then gathers the unknown; negative coefficients may be avoided by gathering the unknown on the opposite side.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Gather pronumerals from both sides, including negative and decimal coefficients and bracketed expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate verbal descriptions into equations, preserving subtraction order and grouped operations, then solve.

questions.mappingNote: Every part requires constructing and solving an equation from words. Parts a–b use one inverse operation; c and g preserve reversed subtraction and collect the unknown positively; d and f use two operations; e undoes multiplication of a sum; h undoes division of a sum; i–j undo addition or subtraction before fractional scaling.
questions.methodNote: Represent the unknown by x and perform equivalent operations on both sides. For subtraction from a known number, move the unknown to obtain a positive coefficient. Undo grouped multiplication or division before isolating x where appropriate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate verbal descriptions into equations, preserving subtraction order and grouped operations, then solve.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate averages into equations, retain exact fractions and collect pronumerals appearing on both sides.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts require modelling a verbal average with an equation. Part (c) additionally requires collecting x terms on one side.
questions.methodNote: Form the average as the sum divided by three. Apply the same operation to both sides, use common denominators for numerical fractions, and isolate the unknown as demonstrated in Examples 3, 4 and 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate averages into equations, retain exact fractions and collect pronumerals appearing on both sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate an average relationship into an equation with the unknown on both sides.

questions.mappingNote: The average is the sum divided by two. Equating it to twice the smaller number creates a linear equation with the unknown on both sides.
questions.methodNote: Perform equivalent operations on both sides, clear the numerical denominator, then collect the unknown on one side, following Examples 3 and 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate an average relationship into an equation with the unknown on both sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Model two sums of consecutive integers with one unknown, equate them, then identify the middle integer.

questions.mappingNote: The equal-sum condition produces a linear equation with the unknown on both sides; modelling the consecutive integers is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides, collect the unknown on one side, and solve using the efficient algebraic steps demonstrated in Example 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model two sums of consecutive integers with one unknown, equate them, then identify the middle integer.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearranges literal equations, including brackets and the subject on both sides.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–m change the subject when it occurs once. Parts n–t gather repeated occurrences and factor out x, so change-subject-appears-twice is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill. As in the teacher answers, displayed quotient solutions assume their denominators are nonzero.
questions.methodNote: Perform equivalent operations on both sides, isolate the unknown, and expand brackets when appropriate. Examples 2–5 support the operation sequence; literal coefficients are retained exactly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearranges literal equations, including brackets and the subject on both sides.

classification.difficultyReason: The sequence progresses from inverse operations with fractional constants to clearing multiple denominators and expanding binomial numerators.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and d use subtraction; b, c, e, f, g, j, m and n use inverse operations with exact fractions; h combines like fractional terms; i and k–l clear denominators; o–t clear denominators, expand where needed and collect terms. The most advanced directly assessed task is solving linear equations with multiple fractions.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides. Example 3 establishes successive inverse operations; Example 5 establishes expansion and collecting terms; Example 6 explicitly permits common denominators or multiplication by the least common multiple.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The sequence progresses from inverse operations with fractional constants to clearing multiple denominators and expanding binomial numerators.

classification.difficultyReason: Literal equations require clearing fractions, collecting terms in x and factorising its coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses subtraction; parts c and d use subtraction or addition followed by multiplication. Parts b and f clear a variable denominator and factorise the coefficient of x. Part e clears all fractions before collecting x. The closest primary catalogue skill is changing the subject when it appears twice.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent operations on both sides, clear denominators, expand brackets where useful, and collect the unknown on one side. Pages 3 and 4 supply the relevant multistep, both-sides and fraction methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Literal equations require clearing fractions, collecting terms in x and factorising its coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Cross multiplication progresses from simple fractions to binomial denominators and collecting unknown terms.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c use constant denominators; d–f introduce x as denominator; g–i introduce binomial numerators; j–l require collecting x terms; m–r require clearing variable denominators and checking excluded values. The closest primary catalogue skill is solving equations with algebraic denominators.
questions.methodNote: Use the explicitly requested cross multiplication, then expand brackets and apply equivalent operations to isolate x. Pages 1–2 establish equivalent operations; page 3 covers collecting unknown terms; page 4 covers expansion and clearing fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Cross multiplication progresses from simple fractions to binomial denominators and collecting unknown terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Cross multiplication of literal equations requires expansion, collecting x terms and factorising x.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b isolate x after clearing denominators. Parts c–f additionally collect and factorise x, making change-subject-appears-twice the closest primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 1–2 establish equivalent operations on both sides; page 3 collects pronumerals on one side; page 4 expands brackets and clears fractions. The question explicitly requires cross multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Cross multiplication of literal equations requires expansion, collecting x terms and factorising x.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent the unknown increase in the numerator while keeping the denominator fixed, then solve a routine linear equation.

questions.mappingNote: The unknown is the amount added to the numerator; the denominator remains 11. This applies the equivalent-operation method demonstrated on teaching page 2.
questions.methodNote: Form an equivalent equation by multiplying both sides by the denominator, then subtract the same number from both sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate an increase in a numerator into an equation and solve exactly.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate an increase in a numerator into an equation and solve with exact fractions.

questions.mappingNote: The unknown is the amount added to the numerator; the denominator remains 3. Modelling the worded condition is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides: multiply by 3, then subtract 2, retaining exact fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate an increase in a numerator into an equation and solve with exact fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Put the same unknown increase in both numerator and denominator, then clear the denominator and collect unknown terms.

questions.mappingNote: The common increase becomes the same unknown in the numerator and denominator. Clearing the denominator gives a linear equation with the unknown on both sides.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides, expand brackets, collect pronumeral terms on one side and isolate the unknown, following Examples 3–6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a shared increase in a numerator and denominator, then solve the resulting equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate an average into an equation and solve using exact fractions.

questions.mappingNote: The question assesses modelling a word problem with an equation; the resulting fractional linear equation uses the inverse operations demonstrated on teaching page 2.
questions.methodNote: Form the average as the sum divided by three, then multiply both sides by three and subtract seven, using the same operation on both sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate an average into an equation and solve using exact fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that adding black sheep changes both the black count and total count, then model the target fraction and solve.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) forms and simplifies the black-sheep fraction. Part (b) models both the numerator and denominator increasing by x, clears the denominator, expands and solves using the methods in Examples 4–6.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent equations by applying the same operation to both sides, expand brackets and collect the unknown on one side.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model the changing number of black sheep and total sheep, then solve the resulting fractional equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Clear the denominator and cancel equal constants, then rearrange the resulting two-variable relationship into the requested ratio.

questions.mappingNote: Question 20 requires clearing a denominator containing a pronumeral before extracting a ratio; this is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides, clear fractions, expand brackets and simplify equivalent equations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear an algebraic denominator, expand and cancel constants, then isolate the requested ratio.

classification.difficultyReason: Proves a general result by clearing algebraic denominators, expanding and cancelling terms, then using the non-zero condition.

questions.mappingNote: The proof applies the taught fraction-clearing and equation-manipulation methods to literal algebraic denominators; the teacher solution confirms cross multiplication followed by cancellation and division by y.
questions.methodNote: Apply equivalent operations to both sides, clear fractions, expand brackets and cancel common terms. Divide only by a non-zero quantity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Proves a general result by clearing algebraic denominators, expanding and cancelling terms, then using the non-zero condition.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires expanding brackets, cancelling variable terms and explaining why an identity has infinitely many solutions.

questions.mappingNote: Question 22 extends the taught simplification method to an identity: the variable terms cancel and the left-hand side equals 6 for every real x.
questions.methodNote: Use LHS and RHS to establish that an equation is true, expanding brackets and collecting like terms as demonstrated in Example 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires expanding brackets, cancelling variable terms and explaining why an identity has infinitely many solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand both sides and interpret the resulting identity as true for every value, rather than expecting a unique numerical solution.

questions.mappingNote: Question 23 applies the bracket-expansion method in Example 5 to an equation with x on both sides; cancellation produces an identity rather than a unique solution.
questions.methodNote: Expand brackets, then perform the same operation on both sides. The definition of a solution requires the equation to be true after substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand both sides and recognise that an identity has infinitely many solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand and cancel the variable terms, then interpret the false constant equality as showing that no value can satisfy the equation.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is solving an equation with the pronumeral on both sides; equal coefficients cancel and leave a contradiction.
questions.methodNote: Expand brackets, then subtract the same variable expression from both sides, following Example 5 and the equivalent-equation operations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand brackets on both sides and recognise that cancellation produces a false equality.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguishes zero, one and infinitely many solutions by considering the coefficient and constants.

questions.mappingNote: Question 25 applies the definition ax+b=c to classify its possible solution counts. The closest catalogue skill is solving one-step equations, with substitution used to verify concrete examples.
questions.methodNote: Use substitution to check proposed coefficients and equivalent operations to isolate the unknown; division requires a non-zero divisor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguishes zero, one and infinitely many solutions by considering the coefficient and constants.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires modelling a two-digit number using place value and restricting the resulting equation to digit values.

questions.mappingNote: Question 26 assesses forming an equation from digital sum and place value. Teacher page 5 confirms the model A+B=(10A+B)/5 and the result 45.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides, clear the numerical denominator, expand brackets and collect terms. Use digit restrictions to identify the two-digit number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires modelling a two-digit number using place value and restricting the resulting equation to digit values.

classification.difficultyReason: Model reversed digits using place value, enumerate all valid digit pairs and prove an impossible increase.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts require modelling a word problem with an equation. Page 3 Example 4 supports collecting pronumerals from both sides; the teacher solution for 27(b) confirms the place-value and divisibility method.
questions.methodNote: Use place-value expressions to model the number and its reversal, then collect like terms by applying equal operations to both sides. Finish with digit restrictions or divisibility.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model reversed digits using place value, enumerate all valid digit pairs and prove an impossible increase.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the order of inverse operations for two-step and grouped inequalities, then translate each result into an endpoint and directed number-line ray.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b use addition or subtraction; c, e and f use positive scaling; d and g–j combine these operations; k and l first divide to undo the grouping, as in Example 3(b). All parts directly assess solving linear inequalities and drawing their number-line solutions.
questions.methodNote: Perform the same operation on both sides to isolate x. Positive multiplication and division preserve the inequality direction. Draw an open endpoint for strict inequalities, a closed endpoint for inclusive inequalities, and a ray in the solution direction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve inequalities using positive multipliers or divisors and represent each solution on a number line.

classification.difficultyReason: Negative coefficients require reversing the inequality; later parts include grouping and numerical denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Every assigned part assesses the negative-number reversal rule directly. Parts a–d isolate a negative multiple of x; e–h first remove a constant; i–j undo a negative grouped multiplier; k–l clear a positive denominator before isolating -x.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides, reversing the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative number. Example 3 uses numerical denominators and grouping, then sketches solutions using open or closed endpoints and directed rays.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Negative coefficients require reversing the inequality; later parts include grouping and numerical denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect pronumeral terms from both sides, expand brackets where needed, and represent inclusive or strict solutions on number lines.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (c) isolate x by collecting terms; (b), (e) and (f) also require division; (d) applies the negative-division rule; (g) and (h) first expand brackets. All eight parts explicitly require number-line representations.
questions.methodNote: Perform the same operation on both sides to isolate the unknown. Reverse the inequality when dividing by a negative number. Use an open endpoint for a strict inequality, a closed endpoint for an inclusive inequality, and a ray toward the satisfying values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect pronumeral terms from both sides, expand brackets where needed, and represent inclusive or strict solutions on number lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange inequalities with literal coefficients, using the given positive sign of a to determine inequality direction.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 applies the positive-operation rules on page 8 and the negative-operation rule and worked sequence on pages 9–10 to literal inequalities. All four parts directly assess solving linear inequalities.
questions.methodNote: Perform the same operations on both sides, preserving direction when dividing by a positive number and reversing direction when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange inequalities with literal coefficients, using the given positive sign of a to determine inequality direction.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve literal inequalities using the given negative sign of a to determine when the inequality reverses.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts apply the negative-number inequality rule to literal coefficients with a known sign. Solving linear inequalities is the directly assessed skill; changing the subject is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Apply equivalent operations to both sides, reversing the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative number; isolate the unknown as in Example 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve literal inequalities using the given negative sign of a to determine when the inequality reverses.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve inequalities with numerical fractions, including collecting variable terms and reversing the inequality after division by a negative coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) apply the positive-operation method of Example 2. Part (c) clears positive numerical denominators and collects variable terms. Part (d) additionally applies the negative-division rule and number-line convention demonstrated in Example 3.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides, clear numerical denominators using a positive multiplier, isolate the unknown, and reverse the inequality when dividing by a negative number. Show strict endpoints as open circles and inclusive endpoints as closed circles, with the ray in the solution direction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve inequalities with numerical fractions, including collecting variable terms and reversing the inequality after division by a negative coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires separate positive and negative denominator cases and reconciliation of their solution sets.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and c follow Example 4(a), allowing both a negative ray and a positive ray. Parts b, d and h follow Example 4(b), with only a bounded positive interval. Parts e, f and g additionally require reversal when dividing by a negative constant; e admits two rays, while f and g admit bounded negative intervals. All eight directly assess rational inequalities by sign cases.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 Example 4 treats x>0 and x<0 separately, reverses the inequality when multiplying by negative x, intersects each result with its case assumption, then combines the valid cases. Pages 8–9 establish equivalent operations and negative-multiplier reversal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires separate positive and negative denominator cases and reconciliation of their solution sets.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve two inequalities with negative coefficients and intersect their solution sets.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 applies the negative-coefficient method demonstrated in Example 3 to two simultaneous conditions; the required number line shows their intersection.
questions.methodNote: Perform the same operation on both sides, reverse the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and represent excluded endpoints with open circles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve two inequalities with negative coefficients and intersect their solution sets.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve two inequalities, reverse one inequality when dividing by a negative number, and intersect their solutions.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 combines two linear inequalities using the methods shown in Examples 2 and 3. Their common solution is represented on a number line.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides; reverse the inequality when dividing by a negative number. Use open endpoints for strict inequalities and closed endpoints for inclusive inequalities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve two inequalities, reverse one inequality when dividing by a negative number, and intersect their solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve two inequalities and identify their common solution.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 applies the taught linear-inequality method twice and requires the intersection because both inequalities must hold.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides, divide by the positive coefficient, and represent the solution with an open endpoint and a leftward ray, following Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve two inequalities and identify their common solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve two inequalities and recognise that their solution sets have no common values.

questions.mappingNote: Question 11 directly assesses solving linear inequalities and recognising an empty intersection.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides to isolate x, then determine whether both resulting conditions can hold. Page 10 explicitly demonstrates rejecting incompatible conditions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve two inequalities and recognise that their solution sets have no common values.

classification.difficultyReason: Count integer ordered pairs satisfying a two-variable inequality; the catalogue skill is the closest match for integer solutions in a region.

questions.mappingNote: The closest catalogue match concerns integer solutions in a region; this task counts integer pairs inside the strict quadratic boundary.
questions.methodNote: The teaching defines solutions as values making an inequality true and demonstrates separating cases. This question requires checking the finite possible integer values, rather than applying linear rearrangement to the squared terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count integer ordered pairs satisfying a two-variable inequality; the catalogue skill is the closest match for integer solutions in a region.

classification.difficultyReason: Applies triangle inequalities to length ranges, exhaustive integer-side enumeration and a greatest integer parameter.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed algebra is solving and combining linear inequalities. Part (b) additionally requires exhaustive integer-side enumeration; part (c) combines three triangle inequalities and an integer restriction.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent inequalities by applying the same operation to both sides, reversing direction when dividing by a negative number. Question 13 supplies the triangle inequality needed for its applications.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies triangle inequalities to length ranges, exhaustive integer-side enumeration and a greatest integer parameter.
